name: transition-property
desc: Chooses which properties a transition watches. The initial value is all, which is why one duration alone animates everything.
body:
A shorthand such as `background` also covers its longhands, because longhands are what actually interpolate. Listing properties instead of `all` keeps unrelated changes from sliding: with `all`, a border colour changed by a theme class animates for no reason.

`none` switches every transition off for the element, which is a quick way to disable motion inside a media query.

name: transition-duration
desc: Sets how long the interpolation runs. Initial value is 0s, so a transition without a duration does nothing.
body: Negative values are invalid and the browser drops the whole declaration. Below one second, milliseconds are easier to compare at a glance. Past roughly 400ms the effect starts to feel like waiting rather than feedback.

name: transition-timing-function
syntax: transition-timing-function: ease | linear | ease-in | ease-out | ease-in-out | cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) | steps(n, end);
desc: Sets the speed curve of the interpolation. Initial value is ease.
body:
`ease-out` decelerates into the destination and suits entrances. `linear` is correct for spinners and progress bars, where a varying speed reads as stutter. In `cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)` the x values must stay between 0 and 1 because time cannot run backwards, while the y values may overshoot to create a bounce without keyframes.

`step-start` equals `steps(1, start)` and `step-end` equals `steps(1, end)`.

name: transition-delay
desc: Waits before the interpolation starts. A negative value starts partway through the curve.

name: transition
desc: Sets property, duration, timing and delay in one declaration. The first time value is the duration and the second is the delay.
body:
Comma separated layers are matched against the longhand lists by position, and a shorter list repeats from its first value.

Important detail: writing `transition` resets all four longhands. A delay set in an earlier rule is cleared by a later shorthand that omits it, because the missing value goes back to `0s`.

name: translate()
desc: Moves the painted box without touching layout. Percentages resolve against the element's own size.
body:
`translateX(-50%)` shifts by half the element's own width, which works at any width, unlike a fixed negative margin. A single argument to `translate` sets x only; y stays at 0.

Translation is independent of `transform-origin`, unlike rotate, scale and skew.

name: scale()
desc: Multiplies the size around the transform origin. Values are unitless factors.
body: Scaling does not reflow, so the element keeps its original slot in the flow and can overlap neighbours. It also does not re-lay out text: a large factor stretches the painted glyphs and they look soft. Keep UI scaling small and animate font size instead when text must genuinely grow.

name: rotate()
desc: Rotates the box clockwise around the transform origin. Accepts deg, rad, grad and turn.
body:
The origin defaults to the centre, so a square rotated by 45 degrees becomes a diamond with even gaps. `rotate(1turn)` and `rotate(360deg)` are the same angle.

Rotating an element that also holds a tooltip moves the tooltip with it, because the whole box is transformed.

name: skew()
desc: Shears the box along one or both axes. Child content is sheared too.

name: transform order
desc: Functions compose left to right, so order changes the result. Keep the list identical at both ends of a transition.
body: Matching function lists interpolate function by function. Mismatched lists are converted to matrices, and the numbers inside the matrix can pass through shapes nobody designed, such as an unintended shrink in the middle of a rotation.

name: transform-origin
desc: Sets the point that rotate, scale and skew act around. Default is 50% 50%, the centre of the border box.
body:
One value sets x and leaves y at the centre. Percentages resolve against the element's own box, so `100% 100%` is the bottom right corner. A third value sets the z position and only matters in 3D.

The property applies to the entire function list, not to a single function. Translation ignores it.

name: perspective
desc: Sets the viewer distance for 3D children, so rotations project with depth instead of looking flat.
body:
Smaller values exaggerate depth. A range of 600px to 1200px reads naturally for cards. `perspective-origin` moves the vanishing point and defaults to the centre of the parent.

Without any perspective, `rotateY` looks like a horizontal squash, which is the usual reason a 3D effect appears broken.

name: transform-style
desc: Keeps children in the parent's 3D space instead of flattening them onto its plane.
body:
The default is `flat`, which projects every child onto the parent's plane. A card flip built from two absolutely positioned faces then shows only one of them, usually the front, mirrored.

Some properties force flattening even when `preserve-3d` is set: `overflow` other than visible, `filter`, `opacity` below 1 and `clip-path` all create a grouping context. Moving `overflow: hidden` off the flip wrapper is often the fix.

name: backface-visibility
desc: Hides the side of an element that faces away from the viewer, which makes two faced cards work.
body: Without it, the front face stays visible through the back after a half turn, so the user reads mirrored text instead of the back content. Older Safari needs the prefixed `-webkit-backface-visibility` beside it.

name: @keyframes
desc: Declares the frames an animation interpolates between. The name is referenced by animation-name.
body:
`from` equals `0%` and `to` equals `100%`, and both forms can be mixed with percentages. Properties missing from every keyframe keep the element's normal style.

Two blocks with the same name do not merge: the later one replaces the earlier completely. Duplicate offsets inside one block merge declaration by declaration.

name: animation-name
desc: Picks which @keyframes block to run. Initial value is none.
body: A misspelled name produces no animation and no console error, so check the spelling first when nothing happens. Two animations on one element must not animate the same property, or the later one in the list wins for the overlap.

name: animation-duration
desc: Time for one pass through the keyframes. Initial value is 0s, so a name without a duration never shows.
body: Negative values are invalid. Entrance animations usually sit between 300ms and 500ms, small feedback under 150ms, and loops are chosen by how much work the loop does rather than by taste.

name: animation-timing-function
desc: Sets the easing between keyframes. It applies per segment, not once across the whole animation.
body: Because the function restarts at each keyframe, `ease-in-out` on a three frame animation slows down at every offset. Declaring the function inside a keyframe overrides it from that offset onward, which is how one block gets two different feels.

name: animation-iteration-count
desc: How many passes run. Fractional values are legal and stop mid pass.
body: `infinite` animations never finish, so `animationend` never fires for them. Anything relying on that event must target a finite animation instead.

name: animation-direction
desc: Chooses which way the timeline is read on each pass.
body: `alternate` flips every second iteration, so an infinite two second animation breathes without a second keyframe block. With `alternate`, `iteration-count: 2` shows one full cycle, because each iteration is a single pass through the timeline.

name: animation-fill-mode
desc: Controls the style before the delay and after the end. Default none, which is why finished entrances snap back.
body:
`forwards` keeps the last keyframe, `backwards` applies the first keyframe during the delay, `both` does the two jobs. Without `both`, a delayed entrance flashes at its natural style and then jumps into the animation.

In a reduced motion block, `animation: none` also cancels the fill, so the end state must exist in a normal declaration.

name: animation-play-state
desc: Freezes or resumes an animation in place.
body: Pausing holds the computed state instead of resetting it, so the element resumes from the same point. This is the standard accessible control for marquees, tickers and any loop that runs longer than a few seconds.

name: animation
syntax: animation: name duration timing delay iteration direction fill-mode play-state;
desc: Sets the animation longhands in one declaration. The first time value is the duration and the second is the delay.
body: Only the name is required, but a missing duration means `0s`, so the animation never becomes visible. Writing the shorthand resets every animation longhand, including `play-state`, which is why a later `animation` declaration undoes an earlier pause.

name: will-change
desc: Hints that a property is about to change, so the browser can promote the element ahead of time.
body: Use it on the element that actually animates, not on every card in a grid. Permanent promotion of many elements costs GPU memory, and on a phone that cost shows up as jank elsewhere. Most transitions and animations run fine without it: modern engines promote elements that are already animating.

name: @media (prefers-reduced-motion)
desc: Matches when the user asked the system to reduce motion. Use it to drop travel and loops while keeping the state change visible.
body:
A near zero duration keeps `transitionend` listeners working while removing the motion. Setting `animation: none` also cancels the fill mode, so the final state has to exist outside the keyframes.

The preference reports a setting, not a capability. A spinner still needs to look busy, so swap a spin for an opacity pulse instead of freezing everything.
